extracted.intended_audience: patent applicants, patent attorneys/representatives, and patent examiners (German jurisdiction / DPMA)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance on procedural and substantive examination of patent applications under the German Patent Act (requests for examination, publication, formalities) and substantive patentability criteria (disclosure, novelty, inventive step, exclusions). Intended for applicants, representatives and examiners in Germany.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exception to patentability for public policy/morality (ordre public)
rubrics_metrics.description: An exception to patentability exists pursuant to section 2(1) of the Patent Act if the intended use of the invention would be contrary to public policy or morality; substantial norms or principles which constitute fundamental principles of the legal and moral order (e.g. fundamental rights, War Weapons Control legislation) may render an invention unpatentable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Not every legal violation constitutes a violation of public order; non-publication may be limited to problematic parts of an application. The DPMA may refrain from publishing parts of an application (or, in exceptional cases, the entire application) that contain information or drawings obviously contrary to ordre public or morality. Non-publication should be limited to the problematic parts unless deletion would leave no informative content.

rubrics_metrics.name: Priority entitlement not examined at obvious-deficiencies stage
rubrics_metrics.description: The substantive entitlement to claim priority – whether domestic or foreign – is not examined during the examination as to obvious deficiencies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Priority entitlement is a substantive issue that is not decided in the 'obvious deficiencies' formal-stage examination; handle priority entitlement at the appropriate substantive stage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reduced time limits for replies in obvious-deficiencies examination
rubrics_metrics.description: In the examination as to obvious deficiencies pursuant to section 42 of the Patent Act, the time limit of four months for answering a communication may be reduced to two months if otherwise the examination cannot be completed before the application is laid open to the public.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examining sections may shorten reply periods to ensure first-publication deadlines are met.

rubrics_metrics.name: Documents used for first publication (Offenlegungsschrift)
rubrics_metrics.description: The originally filed documents must, as a rule, be used for the first publication of the patent application. If documents (e.g. drawings) are missing or unprintable at filing, later-filed compliant documents filed in due time may be incorporated; unsolicited new documents filed later are included in the file but not used for the first publication.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If publication is not based exclusively on documents received on the filing date, a note must be made on the title page stating that the published content is not identical with documents filed on the filing date. If the examination as to obvious deficiencies cannot be concluded before 18 months, uncorrected documents are to be used. If the patent specification has already been published, the application may not be published. German translations may be used for publication if timely filed and compliant with section 14 of the Patent Ordinance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Valid request for examination (section 44)
rubrics_metrics.description: A valid request for examination is a prerequisite for substantive examination under section 44 of the Patent Act; it may be filed by the applicant or any third party until seven years from filing. Processing of the request begins only when the examination fee has been paid.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Any person without residence/office in Germany must appoint a qualified representative entitled to represent in proceedings before the Patent Office. If a prior search request was filed, substantive examination begins only after the search request has been processed. Subsequent duplicate requests are deemed not filed. A third-party requester does not become a party to the examination proceedings but may request file inspection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Formal handling of the request for examination and replies
rubrics_metrics.description: Requests and replies are first examined for formal deficiencies; the case file is passed to the competent examining section which must check competence and forward the file without delay if not competent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The competent examining section adds ancillary classes if necessary. Replies are examined similarly. The request for examination is published in the Patent Gazette. If a third-party request is later found invalid, both the third party and the applicant are notified.

rubrics_metrics.name: Order of processing and priority handling
rubrics_metrics.description: Applications and replies are processed in chronological order of receipt of examination requests/replies, but for efficiency related cases may be jointly processed and the order may be departed from.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Preference may be given where: (a) grant had been promised and grant decision can be taken without delay; (b) applicant has not remedied deficiencies and refusal seems appropriate; (c) preceding communication's deficiencies make it clear that applicant's statements will not change that opinion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Requests for accelerated processing
rubrics_metrics.description: Well-founded requests for accelerated processing should be given preference if it seems possible that normal procedure duration would lead to considerable disadvantages for the requester.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Requests in principle only apply to the next procedural step, but the further procedure may be speeded up if the request so specifies or implies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Subject matter of the examination and required statutory compliance
rubrics_metrics.description: The application must comply with the requirements of sections 34, 37 and 38 of the Patent Act, and the subject matter must be patentable under sections 1 to 5 of the Patent Act. Examination requires interpretation of the patent claim from the point of view of the competent skilled person, using the description and drawings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The subject-matter must be searched based on this interpretation and examined for the explicit grounds for refusal under the Patent Act. Lack of 'clarity' should not be given as a single ground for refusal without interpretation of claims and carrying out a search.

rubrics_metrics.name: Disclosure sufficiency (section 34(4))
rubrics_metrics.description: Pursuant to section 34(4), the application must disclose the invention in a manner sufficiently clear and complete for a person skilled in the art to carry it out. The invention may be disclosed in any part of the application documents except the abstract.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sufficiency requires that the skilled person, using specialist knowledge, can successfully execute the invention. It is sufficient to indicate the decisive direction; at least one practicable way must be disclosed. Tests that do not exceed a reasonable extent are permissible, provided no inventive effort is required. Describing every conceivable variant is unnecessary; however, over-generalisation that merely circumscribes the problem or extends protection beyond the contribution made (e.g., overly broad ranges) is impermissible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claim interpretation from skilled person's point of view
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims must be interpreted from the viewpoint of the competent skilled person, using the description and drawings (see section 14 sentence 2), to determine the semantic content of the claim in its entirety and the contribution of individual features.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This interpretation defines the subject matter to be searched and assessed for patentability; description and drawings must be used where appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Basic patentability requirements (sections 1–5)
rubrics_metrics.description: Pursuant to section 1(1), patents are granted only to inventions which are new, involve an inventive step and are susceptible of industrial application; inventions must relate to a field of technology.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Technical character typically involves systematic teaching applying controllable natural forces to achieve predictable results, but technical character may also arise from knowledge based on technical considerations and its implementation. Reasons must be given for assessing a feature as non-technical. A claim combining technical and non-technical features is as a rule eligible for protection, but non-technical features must not be taken into account for inventive step assessment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Excluded subject matter (section 1(3)) and caveat
rubrics_metrics.description: The following are not considered inventions as such and are generally not patentable: discoveries, scientific theories and mathematical methods; aesthetic creations; schemes, rules and methods for mental acts, playing games or doing business and computer programs; presentation of information.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The exclusion applies only to these items 'as such' — if a teaching contains instructions to solve a specific technical problem with technical means (a particular implementation), the exclusion does not apply. Implementations dominating a technical solution can render the subject matter patentable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exclusion for medical/surgical/diagnostic methods (section 2a(1))
rubrics_metrics.description: Particularly methods for the treatment of the human or animal body by surgery or therapy and diagnostic methods practised on the human or animal body are excluded from patent protection (section 2a(1) number 2).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A combination of technical and non-technical features may still be patentable, but multi-step methods are not patentable as a whole pursuant to section 2a(1) number 2 if one of the steps includes a method of surgery, therapy or diagnosis.

rubrics_metrics.name: State of the art definition (section 3)
rubrics_metrics.description: The state of the art comprises any knowledge made available to the public by written or oral description, by use, or in any other way before the relevant priority date. Contents of certain earlier patent applications (national, European with DE designation, PCT where DE is designated) as originally filed are considered part of the state of the art.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The entire content of earlier applications is state of the art irrespective of whether a patent was granted for them. Disclosures within six months before filing due to evident abuse or display at official exhibitions may be disregarded if conditions (timely statement and certificate) are met.

rubrics_metrics.name: Novelty assessment (section 3)
rubrics_metrics.description: During novelty examination it must be determined whether the subject matter differs in any respect from each individual prior publication or prior use. The subject matter is deemed new if each individual comparison shows at least one feature not comprised in the prior art; novelty is denied only if all claimed features can be inferred from a single citation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The entire content of the prior teaching is relevant, and implicit disclosures may be 'read into' a document only if they are self-evident to the skilled person; one cannot add specialist knowledge beyond what the document discloses. Earlier applications’ content relevant for priority is to be considered; known substances may be patentable for a new therapeutic use (second medical indication) under section 3(3)/(4).

rubrics_metrics.name: Inventive step assessment (section 4)
rubrics_metrics.description: An invention involves an inventive step if, having regard to the state of the art, it is not obvious to a person skilled in the art. The assessment must be made on the basis of the state of the art available before the priority date, from the skilled person's perspective and avoiding a retrospective approach.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Define the competent skilled person (typically the developer, not the user). The skilled person must have had reason or a suggestion to choose the claimed solution. General expert knowledge may provide a reason in context, but its general suitability alone is not sufficient. Courts have not developed universally applicable specific criteria; case law can serve only as guidance. Auxiliary/post-hoc criteria may only in individual cases justify a critical review.

rubrics_metrics.name: Role and definition of the person skilled in the art
rubrics_metrics.description: For assessments of disclosure, novelty and inventive step, the relevant skilled person must be defined; the skilled person’s perspective is used to interpret claims, determine what is self-evident in prior art, and assess obviousness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The skilled person is the one who would normally be assigned the technical task. If ascertained knowledge comes from another technical field it may be doubtful whether it belongs to that skilled person's knowledge. Teams of experts or consultations may be considered where appropriate.
